item.title: The Harvesters
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: This is one of the first great paintings in Western art where ordinary life is the whole subject — no saints, no gods, no kings. Bruegel painted it as part of a series depicting the months of the year (six panels, of which five survive); this one, likely July and August, shows the wheat harvest at full heat. Some peasants scythe and bundle; others sprawl under a pear tree eating bread and porridge, and one is fast asleep with his legs flung apart. The genius is the air itself: that hazy, golden late-summer atmosphere that you can almost feel on your skin, receding across fields to a distant harbor. Painted for the suburban villa of an Antwerp merchant, the series treated the rhythm of labor and season — not scripture — as worthy of monumental art, and landscape painting was never the same.
item.lookFor: Follow the path cut through the wheat at lower left: it funnels you into the picture the way a footpath does in life, one of Bruegel's favorite tricks for making you a participant instead of a spectator.
